messages.body_plain:
Hi James,

Sorry for late response.

First. about scope of conclusion : for label-free data, only restricted or expanded scope of subject replicates can be used. Because for label-free data, subject and MS runs are the same, can't separate MS run variation. Therefore, if you use expanded scope of technical replicate (MS run), the result is the same with restrict scope of technical replicate.

Second. about expanded scope of conclusion with unequal feature variance : If you use expanded technical scope with unequal feature variance, the result would be restricted scope of subject with unequal feature variance. (because there is no consider for scope of technical replicate for label-free data. Currently, expanded scope of conclusion with unequal feature variance can't be implemented in MSstats due to some technical difficulty.

Third, Sorry for really late response for your comment in MSstats github. We really appreciate for your comment. We welcome patches. The next MSstats.daily version, which will be released next week, fix the the bug you mentioned.

Thank you.

Meena

messages.subject: [FAQ] scope of conclusion for label-free analysis
messages.subject_clean: [FAQ] scope of conclusion for label-free analysis
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

We got several same questions about scope of conclusion for label-free analysis. Here is the summary.

1. No scope of conclusion for MS runs : If you don't have technical replicates, MS run is the combination of Subject and condition. So, there is no extra MS run. Therefore, we can consider only scope of conclusion for biological replicates (Subject). If you have technical replicates, the error from technical replicates is pooled into the random error (in statistical terms). So, we can use restricted or expanded scope of conclusion for biological replicate for label-free analysis.

2. scope of conclusion and feature variance
     1) equal feature variance with restricted scope of biological replicate : okay
     2) equal feature variance with expanded scope of biological replicate : okay
     3) unequal feature variance with restricted scope of biological replicate : okay
     4) unequal feature variance with expanded scope of biological replicate : not implemented in MSstats yet

hope to be clear for everyone.
-Meena

messages.subject: [FAQ] iTRAC and SILAC data analysis
messages.subject_clean: [FAQ] iTRAC and SILAC data analysis
messages.body_plain:
Here is another frequent question about iTRAQ or SILAC data analysis from users. Below is one of the response from Prof. Olga Vitek,

-------------------------------
For SILAC experiments, where a reference sample is added to every endogenous sample in a constant concentration, MSstats can be used as is. We recommend to look at the profile plots to have a sense of the nature of interferences, and remove run x feature (and possibly condition x feature) interactions if the interferences appear random.

For SILAC experiments where two endogenous samples (e.g. one from each group) are mixed together, MSstats should be applicable in principle. However we haven't had a chance to benchmark it thoroughly, we plan to do this shortly.

For TMT and iTRAQ things are more complicated, since the quantification occurs at the MS2 level, and MS2 spectra create an additional blocking structure. We currently do not account for this in the model. We plan to investigate this in the future, however it will likely to take some time.
--------------------------------

- Meena

messages.subject: Re: Error - Group Comparison
messages.subject_clean: Error - Group Comparison
messages.body_plain:
Dear Vendula,

I will let Meena respond on the error messages. Meanwhile, I have one comment. You mentioned that in your dataset different conditions have a different number of replicates. This makes me think that each condition is measured on distinct biological replicates (e.g. people, animals, cell line batches etc). Is this correct?

If my interpretation is correct, then you have what we call a 'Group comparison' design. This design requires that each biological replicate (i.e. person, animal etc) have a distinct BioReplicate id. E.g, if your experiment included a total of 10 people in all conditions combined, you should have 10 distinct BioReplicate ids.

In your dataset, multiple conditions have the same BioReplicate. E.g., for peptide GTFIIDPGGVIR fragment Y9, BioReplicate 1 appears in 10 conditions. This makes MSstats think that the same biological replicate (person/animal...) could be observed in all the conditions. Then MSstats fits a different model for the 'Time course design' and not for the 'Group comparison design'. If the number of runs per condition varies, and if the experiment has missing values, the time course model can be quite complicated, and may require a lot of memory.

I suggest that you double-check that you correctly specify the BioReplicate ids. Please check user manual for more details.

Sincerely
Olga

I tried to draw the profile plot, and I couldn't find the case you mentioned. Could you explain with some specific case?

4. normalization for label-free SRM : I generally do not recommend equalize median or quantile normalization for label-free SRM. When I say 'large' number of proteins, I generally means several thousands. Less than 100 proteins is not large number for me, even though you expect few of them to change. So, I recommend use global standards with protein or peptides that you know that they should be equal amount across all samples or that you already spike-in the same amount during sample processing step. and I just found that data seems fractionation. in this case, there are less number of peptides per run. so, equalize median and quantile normalization shouldn't be used.

5. p-value : first zero p-value in result is not actually zero, but very very small value, really close to zero. and There is no answer for how many or what proportion of proteins are significant. It really depends on your experiment. If you already checked the profile plot and result together, and it seems reliable, I think that it is not huge problem for analysis. However, just one comment, I don't know how many peptide per protein and how many transitions per peptide you used and how profile plot looks like or how the quality of data is. If you have quite large number of them in a proteins and there is not much variation across features, p-values could be less. If features are quite parallel across condition, you can use 'interference=FALSE" in groupComparison function in R or uncheck 'Include interference transition' in MSstats Group Comparison window in external tool.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Linda,

>From the description, it appears that your input data file is still structured incorrectly.

Your key comment was that, for each of the 2 groups and 3 biological replicates per group, the peptides were targeted in 3 different transition lists. The different transition lists are called 'methods' in the language of Skyline and MSstats, and are very important. Essentially, MSsats needs to know that each transition list was acquired separately.

Currently MSstats mistakes multiple methods for repeated measurements of a same biological replicate under multiple conditions (hence the message 'time course'). Since not every method is acquired in every condition, MSstats thinks that there are many missing values. The profile plots therefore do not produce lines. And MSstats attempts to fill in the missing values according to its interpretation of the design. This is incorrect. Please see bullet (i) on page 8 of the user manual for a description of how to set up different methods. A correct setup will produce profile plots with lines.

Regarding the scope of biological replication: it is determined with respect to the number of biological replicates, not with respect to the number of proteins. Since you have only 3 biological replicates per group, reduced scope of biological replication is appropriate. However keep in mind that you will likely have many false positive differences. Expanded scope of biological replication always results in more conservative (but more reproducible) results. However it typically requires a larger number of biological replicate than what you have.

HTH
Olga

    sparseDataTemp$Peptide <- paste(sparseDataTemp$PeptideSequence,

    sparseDataTemp$Transition <- paste(sparseDataTemp$FragmentIon,

    sparseDataTemp$Transition <- factor(sparseDataTemp$Transition)
    sparseDataTemp$Group_Original <- factor(sparseDataTemp$Group_Original)
    sparseDataTemp$Subject_Original <- factor(sparseDataTemp$Subject_Original)
    sparseDataTemp$Run <- as.numeric(factor(sparseDataTemp$Run))
    sparseDataTemp <- sparseDataTemp[, c("Protein", "Peptide",

    sparseDataTemp <- sparseDataTemp[with(sparseDataTemp, order(Group_Original,
        Subject_Original, Label)), ]
    sparseDataTemp$Run <- factor(sparseDataTemp$Run, levels = unique(sparseDataTemp$Run),
        labels = seq(1, length(unique(sparseDataTemp$Run))))
    unique(sparseDataTemp[, c("Group_Original", "Run")])
    if (qualityControlPlot == TRUE) {
        sparseDataCAP <- sparseDataTemp
        colnames(sparseDataCAP) <- c("PROTEIN", "PEPTIDE", "TRANSITION",
            "FEATURE", "LABEL", "GROUP_ORIGINAL", "SUBJECT_ORIGINAL",
            "RUN", "ABUNDANCE")
        .QualityControlPlot_ProfilePlots(sparseDataCAP, address,
            featureName = "Peptide")
        .QualityControlPlot_Boxplots(sparseDataCAP, address)
    }
    if (nlevels(sparseDataTemp$Peptide) > nlevels(sparseRefPep)) {
        result <- .imputeAnalyze(sparseDataTemp, sparseRefPep)
        ImputeData <- result$data
        ImputeData <- ImputeData[, c("Protein", "Peptide", "Transition",

        save(ImputeData, file = paste(address, "ImputeData.RData",

    }
    if (nlevels(sparseDataTemp$Peptide) == nlevels(sparseRefPep)) {

        ImputeData$Intensity <- ImputeData$Intensity100
        ImputeData$impute_Intensity <- ImputeData$Intensity100
        ImputeData$index_Intensity <- FALSE
        ImputeData$postVar <- 1
        ImputeData$sampleVar <- 1
        ImputeData$weight <- 1
        check <- which(colnames(ImputeData) %in% c("Group", "Subject"))
        if (length(check) > 0) {
            ImputeData <- ImputeData[, -which(colnames(ImputeData) %in%
                c("Group", "Subject"))]
        }
        ImputeData <- data.frame(ImputeData, Group = 0, Subject = 0)
        ImputeData$Group[ImputeData$Label == "L"] <- ImputeData$Group_Original[ImputeData$Label ==
            "L"]
        ImputeData$Group <- factor(ImputeData$Group)
        ImputeData[ImputeData$Label == "L", "Subject"] <- ImputeData$Subject_Original[ImputeData$Label ==
            "L"]
        ImputeData$Subject <- factor(ImputeData$Subject)
        ImputeData$Run <- factor(ImputeData$Run)
        ImputeData <- data.frame(ImputeData, Subject_Nested = paste(ImputeData[,
            "Group"], ImputeData[, "Subject"], sep = "."))
        temp <- unique(ImputeData[, c("Group", "Subject")])
        temp <- temp[with(temp, order(Group, Subject)), ]
        temp <- data.frame(temp, Subject_Nested = paste(temp[,
            "Group"], temp[, "Subject"], sep = "."))
        ImputeData$Subject_Nested <- factor(ImputeData$Subject_Nested,
            levels = temp$Subject_Nested)
        ImputeData <- ImputeData[, c("Protein", "Peptide", "Transition",
            "Feature", "Label", "Group_Original", "Subject_Original",
            "Run", "Intensity100", "Intensity", "impute_Intensity",
            "index_Intensity", "Group", "Subject", "Subject_Nested",
            "postVar", "sampleVar", "weight")]
        save(ImputeData, file = paste(address, "ImputeData.RData",
            sep = ""))
    }
    temp <- .groupComparisonAnalyze(ImputeData, comparison, scope)
    TestResult <- temp$result
    FittedData <- temp$data
    save(FittedData, file = paste(address, "FittedData.RData",
        sep = ""))
    save(TestResult, file = paste(address, "TestResult.RData",
        sep = ""))
    if (evaluationPlot == TRUE) {
        .Evaluation_ResidualPlots(FittedData, address)
        .Evaluation_PredictionPlots(ImputeData, sparseRefPep,
            address)
    }
}
